newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech gov't moves to protect debt-ridden hospitals.
newsitem.headline: Czech gov't moves to protect debt-ridden hospitals.

text.p: The Czech health ministry said on Tuesday it would petition a commercial court for a three-month protection period for two large Czech hospitals threatened with foreclosure by creditors.

Health Minister Jan Strasky told a news conference that the debts, reportedly totalling about one billion crowns, were to a large extent caused by poor cost control at the hospitals, Vseobecna Fakultni Nemocnice and Fakultni Nemocnice Motol.

The ministry jumped into the deepening financial troubles of hospitals, saying it would close clinics, lower capacity and freeze investment expenditure, until problems throughout the system are resolved.
The ministry announced the action following last week's demands of creditors to foreclose on the two Prague hospitals who are heavily in debt.
Strasky said the two hospitals would use the protection period to pull its cash flow into balance under "stiff supervision" of the ministry.
But he rejected calls by the Czech Association of Hospitals to simply pay off debts of most of the country's medical centres, estimated at around five billion crowns.
"I cannot imagine the state giving some extra money to large hospitals... Audits have shown that they sometimes even lack proper acounting," Strasky told reporters.
He said that the hospitals should decrease their excessive capacities and sell some property.
Doctors and hospitals are paid in a fee for service system by insurance companies which are financed by a mandatory 13.5 percent deduction from salaries and private income.
For pensioners, children and the unemployed, contributions are paid by the state.

This formula has led to a large increase of the number of treatments, boosting costs and sinking several of the originally 27 health insurers who left extensive debts behind, but still sending most hospitals into the red.
The government has been mulling a total overhaul in financing the health care system to make it self-sufficient, but no proposal has been approved.
